title: Can Theology Be a Science? Aquinas on Borrowed Starting Points

source.title: Summa Theologiae, First Part, Question 1: The nature and extent of sacred doctrine
source.venue: Second and Revised Edition, 1920, literally translated by Fathers of the English Dominican Province (New Advent online edition)

intro.summary: Thomas Aquinas asks whether, besides philosophy built by human reason, people need a 'sacred doctrine' taught by divine revelation. He also asks whether that doctrine counts as a real science and how it may argue. He works through ten short debates, each answering objections. He concludes that revelation is needed, even for truths reason could reach. He holds that sacred doctrine is a genuine science, because it starts from principles borrowed from a higher knowledge, just as music borrows from arithmetic, and it argues from those principles rather than proving them. The main limitation is that the whole case rests on premises the text takes from faith, such as that Scripture is revealed by God, so it persuades only readers who grant them; many modern philosophers reject both those premises and his older, Aristotelian sense of 'science'. This lesson leaves out several articles that would make good follow-ups: whether the doctrine is speculative or practical (Article 4), its rank and its relation to wisdom (Articles 5–6), why Scripture uses lowly metaphors (Article 9), and the four senses of Scripture (Article 10).
background: Aquinas was a 13th-century Christian friar and teacher who tried to show how faith and Aristotle's philosophy fit together.
In his time, 'science' (Latin scientia) meant any organised body of knowledge that reasons from first principles to conclusions, not only lab experiments.
'Revelation' means truths that Christians believe God made known, mainly through the Bible, rather than truths people worked out for themselves.
The Summa Theologiae is written as a long series of short debates, each called an 'article'.
intro.aha: Aquinas claims theology can be a real science without proving its own starting points, just as music borrows from arithmetic, so it argues from them, not to them, and against someone who grants none of them it can only answer objections.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Philosophy uses human reason to study everything, and it even includes a branch about God. So why would anyone need a second kind of knowledge on top of it? Aquinas opens his great textbook by testing that challenge. He states the objection in its strongest form before answering it.
primer.quote: It seems that, besides philosophical science, we have no need of any further knowledge.

primer.heading: What he did
primer.body: Aquinas splits the big question into ten smaller ones, called articles. Examples are: is this doctrine necessary, is it a science, is God its subject, may it use argument? Each article lists objections, gives a counter-authority, states his own answer and then replies to each objection in turn. His tools are everyday comparisons: an astronomer and a physicist proving the same fact, a musician trusting a mathematician, eyes that see every coloured thing.

primer.heading: What he found: revelation is needed
primer.body: Some truths about God lie beyond reason entirely, so they must be revealed. Aquinas adds a less obvious point. Even truths that reason could reach would, left to reason alone, reach too few people, too late and mixed with mistakes.
primer.quote: because the truth about God such as reason could discover, would only be known by a few, and that after a long time, and with the admixture of many errors.

primer.heading: What he found: a science with borrowed starting points
primer.body: An objector says a science must start from self-evident truths, and articles of faith are not self-evident. Aquinas answers that some sciences start from principles proven elsewhere. Music, for example, takes its principles from arithmetic. Sacred doctrine is that kind of science: it takes its starting points from God's own knowledge and reasons onward from them.
primer.quote: So it is that sacred doctrine is a science because it proceeds from principles established by the light of a higher science, namely, the science of God and the blessed.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: This sets a rule for debate. Theology argues from its principles, not to them. With someone who accepts some revealed truths, you can argue from those. With someone who accepts none, you can only answer their objections. Aquinas thinks no objection can ever be a true proof against faith. That last step assumes faith is true, so it convinces only those who already grant his starting points. Critics then and now dispute it.
primer.quote: Since faith rests upon infallible truth, and since the contrary of a truth can never be demonstrated, it is clear that the arguments brought against faith cannot be demonstrations, but are difficulties that can be answered.

concepts.title: How a medieval debate is built
concepts.idea: Each article tests a yes/no question by stating objections, citing a counter-authority, giving the author's answer, and then replying to each objection one by one.

terms.means: One short unit of the Summa that settles a single yes-or-no question, such as 'Whether sacred doctrine is a science?'
An argument for the view the author will end up rejecting, set out fairly at the start and usually opening with 'It seems that…'
A short citation of an authority, often a Bible verse, that points the other way from the objections
The author's answer to one particular objection, given after his main answer, so each opposing point is dealt with in turn

concepts.recap: An article runs question → objections → 'On the contrary' → 'I answer that' → replies, so the other side's best arguments are heard first and then each one is answered.

understand.explanation: Each article of the Summa takes one yes-or-no question and tests it in a fixed order, a debating format of the medieval schools (scholasticism). First come the objections: arguments for the view Aquinas will reject, stated before he says anything, and usually opening with 'It seems that'. Then a passage marked On the contrary (sed contra) cites an authority, often a Bible verse, that points the other way; it signals a direction but is not yet his full argument. Next, 'I answer that' gives Aquinas's own position and his reasons, and this can be more careful than either side: in Article 4 the objections say sacred doctrine is practical, 'On the contrary' says it is speculative, and his answer is that it includes both but is mainly speculative. Finally each objection gets its own reply to an objection, much as a careful judge answers every point the losing side raised, though sometimes (as in Article 4) one sentence covers them all.
understand.quote: Article 1. Whether, besides philosophy, any further doctrine is required? Objection 1. It seems that, besides philosophical science, we have no need of any further knowledge.

activities.title: Article 1, part by part

steps.text: The question. The article opens: 'Whether, besides philosophy, any further doctrine is required?' Philosophy here means knowledge built by human reason alone. The question can only be answered yes or no.

Objection 1. 'It seems that, besides philosophical science, we have no need of any further knowledge.' The reason given: Scripture says not to seek things too high for us, and everything not above reason is already covered by philosophy.
steps.result: An argument for 'No', which Aquinas will answer

steps.text: Objection 2 opens with 'Further'. Everything that exists is studied by philosophy, even God, since Aristotle described a philosophical 'theology'. So again, nothing more is needed.

On the contrary (sed contra). Aquinas quotes 2 Timothy 3:16: 'All Scripture, inspired of God is profitable to teach…' Scripture inspired by God is not part of philosophy, so some other knowledge is useful.
steps.result: An authority pointing to 'Yes', short and not yet the full case

steps.text: I answer that. Now Aquinas speaks in his own voice: 'It was necessary for man's salvation that there should be a knowledge revealed by God besides philosophical science built up by human reason.' He then gives his reasons. (Later concepts look at those reasons in detail.)

Each reply to an objection comes last. Reply to Objection 1 answers the first objection: things beyond reason should not be hunted for by reason, but once God reveals them they are accepted by faith. Reply to Objection 2 answers the second: sciences differ by how they know, not only by what they study.
steps.result: Each 'No' argument gets its own answer, in order

activities.takeaway: The article never starts with Aquinas's view. It starts with the case against it, and it is only finished once every one of those arguments has been answered.

activities.prompt: Put the five parts of an article in the order Aquinas always uses.
items: On the contrary: an authority pointing the other way
I answer that: Aquinas's own position and reasons
Replies to the objections, one by one
hints: Aquinas lets the opposing side speak before he does.
His own answer has to come before he can reply to anyone, because the replies lean on it.
The short authority sits between the case against and Aquinas's own answer.
activities.explanation: The question sets the yes/no issue. The objections state the case Aquinas will reject, so it is heard first and in its strongest form. 'On the contrary' gives a short authority for the other side. 'I answer that' is the heart of the article, where Aquinas argues his own position. The replies come last because each one applies that answer to a specific objection.

activities.title: Which part is this?
activities.prompt: These sentences come from other articles of the same Question. The labels have been removed. Sort each one into the part of the article it comes from.

cards.text: It seems that sacred doctrine is not a science. For every science proceeds from self-evident principles.
cards.feedback: Objection (Article 2). The signal 'It seems that' opens an argument for the view Aquinas goes on to reject. He concludes that sacred doctrine is a science.

cards.text: Further, no science deals with individual facts. But this sacred science treats of individual facts, such as the deeds of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and such like.
cards.feedback: Objection (Article 2, Objection 2). 'Further' is how each objection after the first begins, adding one more argument against Aquinas's view.

cards.text: Holy Scripture speaks of it as one science: "Wisdom gave him the knowledge [scientiam] of holy things" (Wisdom 10:10).
cards.feedback: On the contrary (Article 3). It is a short appeal to an authority, a Bible verse, with no extended argument. That is the mark of the 'On the contrary'.

cards.text: Other sciences are called the handmaidens of this one: "Wisdom sent her maids to invite to the tower" (Proverbs 9:3).
cards.feedback: On the contrary (Article 5). Again it is a single cited verse pointing against the objections, not Aquinas's own reasoning.

cards.text: Sacred doctrine is a science. We must bear in mind that there are two kinds of sciences.
cards.feedback: I answer that (Article 2). It states a yes, so it can look like 'On the contrary', but it cites no authority. Aquinas speaks in his own voice and begins to explain ('We must bear in mind…'). That makes it his main answer.

cards.text: It is befitting Holy Writ to put forward divine and spiritual truths by means of comparisons with material things.
cards.feedback: I answer that (Article 9). It is Aquinas's own position on whether Scripture should use metaphors, and he goes on to give his reasons. It answers the whole question, not one particular objection.

cards.text: Individual facts are treated of in sacred doctrine, not because it is concerned with them principally, but they are introduced rather both as examples to be followed in our lives (as in moral sciences)…
cards.feedback: Reply (Article 2, Reply to Objection 2). It takes up the exact point of one objection, about individual facts such as Abraham's deeds, and shows why that point fails. A reply aims at one objection, not at the whole question.

cards.text: Poetry makes use of metaphors to produce a representation, for it is natural to man to be pleased with representations. But sacred doctrine makes use of metaphors as both necessary and useful.
cards.feedback: Reply (Article 9, Reply to Objection 1). That objection said metaphors belong to poetry, 'the least of all the sciences'. This sentence answers that specific claim, so it is a reply.

hints: Look for signals: 'It seems that' and 'Further' open objections, and a lone cited verse usually means 'On the contrary'.
If a sentence answers the whole question in Aquinas's own voice, it is 'I answer that'. If it answers one particular argument, it is a reply.
Two cards argue against sacred doctrine being a science. They are the objections Aquinas is about to answer.
activities.takeaway: Each part has a job. Objections argue for the view to be rejected. 'On the contrary' cites an authority for the other side. 'I answer that' gives Aquinas's reasoned position. Each reply answers one objection. Once you can spot the job, you can read any article.

concepts.title: Same fact, different route
concepts.idea: Sciences are told apart by how they know, not by what they study, so the same truth can belong to two different sciences.

terms.means: For Aquinas, any organised body of knowledge that reasons from its own starting points. It is wider than today's laboratory science.
The route by which a science reaches its conclusions, such as mathematics, observing matter, natural reason or revelation
Aquinas's name for the body of knowledge received through God's revelation, as opposed to knowledge built up by human reason alone

concepts.recap: What makes two sciences different is the route each takes to its knowledge. So reason and revelation can teach the same truth and still be different sciences.

understand.explanation: In Article 1, an objector argues that philosophy already studies everything, even God, so a second body of knowledge about God would be pointless. Aquinas answers that a science (scientia), meaning any organised body of knowledge that reasons from its own starting points rather than only laboratory science, is told apart by its means of knowing: the route it takes to reach its conclusions, not just the topic it talks about. His example is the astronomer and the physicist: both can prove the earth is round, one by mathematics and the other by studying physical matter. In the same way, a truth about God can be reached by human reason, in the theology that is part of philosophy, and also taught by revelation, in sacred doctrine, and these two are different kinds of science. This is Aquinas's way of dividing the sciences, not a rule that everyone accepts; many today group fields by their subject instead.
understand.quote: Sciences are differentiated according to the various means through which knowledge is obtained. For the astronomer and the physicist both may prove the same conclusion: that the earth, for instance, is round: the astronomer by means of mathematics (i.e. abstracting from matter), but the physicist by means of matter itself.

activities.prompt: Two experts reach one conclusion: the earth is round. Look at how each one gets there.

cases.label: The astronomer
cases.text: Proves the earth is round by mathematics. They reason about shape and figure while setting aside what the earth is made of. Aquinas calls this 'abstracting from matter'.

cases.label: The physicist
cases.text: Proves the same thing 'by means of matter itself', reasoning from the physical stuff of the earth. Aquinas gives no further detail of the proof here.

activities.takeaway: The conclusion is the same, but the means of knowing is different. For Aquinas, that is what makes astronomy and physics two separate sciences. Medieval scholars already took the earth's roundness as known, so this is his illustration, not a new discovery.

activities.prompt: Now apply the same test to knowledge about God.

cases.label: Theology inside philosophy
cases.text: Reaches truths about God by natural reason alone. Following Aristotle, the objector calls it 'theology, or the divine science', a part of philosophy.

cases.label: Sacred doctrine
cases.text: Receives truths about God through revelation and accepts them by faith. Aquinas grants that some of these truths are ones reason could also reach.

activities.takeaway: Even where the two teach the same truth, Aquinas concludes they 'differ in kind', because one knows by reason and the other by revelation. Why revelation was needed at all is the next concept.

activities.title: How do you know that?
activities.prompt: Each card is an everyday claim and the way someone came to know it. Sort each card by its route, not by its topic.

cards.text: The table is 2 metres long: I ran a tape measure along it.
cards.feedback: The tape touches the table itself. This is direct measurement, a little like the physicist working 'by means of matter itself'.

cards.text: The table is 2 metres long: it covers 8 floor tiles, each 25 cm, and 8 × 25 cm = 2 m.
cards.feedback: It is the same fact as the tape-measure card, but reached by arithmetic from other facts. The route differs even though the conclusion does not.

cards.text: The table is 2 metres long: the shop's catalogue says so.
cards.feedback: It is the same fact a third time, now accepted on the word of a source you trust. The topic never changed. Only the route did.

cards.text: The bath water is 40 °C: I read it off a thermometer.
cards.feedback: A thermometer reads the water directly, so this is measurement.

cards.text: My phone bill is €30: I added up the three charges on it.
cards.feedback: You worked the total out from other numbers. The total comes from calculation, even though the charges themselves came from the bill.

cards.text: Sunset is at 18:40 today: the weather service announced it.
cards.feedback: You did not observe or compute this yourself. You accepted it from a source you trust.

activities.takeaway: The table's length appeared in all three groups. What decided the group was how it was known, which is Aquinas's test in miniature. This is only an everyday analogy: his 'sciences' are whole organised bodies of knowledge, not single claims.
hints: Ignore what the claim is about and ask how the person came to know it.
Did they touch the thing, work it out from other facts, or take someone's word?

activities.question: The objector says philosophy already treats of God, so a second science of God is superfluous. Which reply matches Aquinas's answer in Article 1?

options.text: The same truths can be reached by a different means, revelation rather than reason, so the second science is a different kind and not redundant.
options.feedback: Correct. He grants the overlap in subject and locates the difference in the means of knowing: theology in sacred doctrine 'differs in kind' from the theology that is part of philosophy.

options.text: Philosophy gets God wrong, so it must be replaced by revelation.
options.feedback: Aquinas does not say this here. He allows that things 'may be learned from philosophical science, so far as they can be known by natural reason'. His point is about a different route, not about replacing philosophy.

options.text: Sacred doctrine studies a completely different topic from philosophy, so the two never overlap.
options.feedback: This misses his point. The astronomer and the physicist prove the very same conclusion. The overlap is allowed, and the difference lies in how each knows.

options.text: Two sciences can never prove the same conclusion, so one of them must be dropped.
options.feedback: This is the opposite of his example. He says both may prove the same conclusion, that the earth is round, by different means.

hints: Recall the astronomer and the physicist. Did they disagree about the conclusion?

activities.question: A letter is shown to date from about 1850. A historian proves it from the events the letter mentions. A chemist proves it by testing the ink. By Aquinas's test, what follows?

options.text: They work in different sciences, because each reaches the date by a different means.
options.feedback: Correct. This is the astronomer and physicist pattern again: one conclusion reached by two routes, so two sciences.

options.text: They work in the same science, because they reach the same conclusion.
options.feedback: This sorts by conclusion, not by route. Aquinas's test looks at the means through which knowledge is obtained, and these means differ.

options.text: One of them must be mistaken, because two sciences cannot prove the same thing.
options.feedback: Aquinas says plainly that two sciences 'may prove the same conclusion'. Agreement between different routes is no sign of error.

options.text: Only the chemist counts as a science, because only the chemist measures something physical.
options.feedback: This uses today's narrow sense of 'science'. For Aquinas, mathematics-based astronomy is a science too, and so is any organised reasoning from its own starting points.

hints: Which matters for Aquinas: the conclusion, or the route to it?

concepts.title: Why reason alone was not enough
concepts.idea: Revelation is needed both for truths beyond reason and for truths within reason that would otherwise be known only by a few, after a long time, and mixed with errors.

terms.means: In Aquinas's usage, the final goal something is aimed at, like the finish line of a race
In Christian belief, being brought safely to that final goal: life with God

concepts.recap: Revelation was needed twice over: for truths reason can never reach, and for truths reason could reach but only for a few, slowly and with errors.

understand.explanation: In Article 1, Aquinas asks whether people need any knowledge besides philosophy, and he answers yes for two separate reasons. First, he says humans are directed to God as their "end", meaning the final goal of their life, and this goal lies beyond what reason can grasp; since you must know a goal before you can steer your thoughts and actions toward it, truths beyond reason had to be revealed. Second, even truths about God that reason could in principle work out would, left to reason alone, be known only by a few people, after a long time, and mixed with many errors. Because "salvation", in Christian belief being brought safely to that final goal, depends on this knowledge, Aquinas concludes that revelation brings it to people "more fitly and more surely". Keep in mind what kind of claim this is: an argument made from inside Christian faith, not a measured finding, and a reader who does not grant its first step (that humans are directed to God) will not be bound by its conclusion.
understand.quote: Hence it was necessary for the salvation of man that certain truths which exceed human reason should be made known to him by divine revelation. Even as regards those truths about God which human reason could have discovered, it was necessary that man should be taught by a divine revelation; because the truth about God such as reason could discover, would only be known by a few, and that after a long time, and with the admixture of many errors.

activities.prompt: Trace Aquinas's first reason, step by step, from where he starts to his conclusion. Some boxes are side roads: they appear in the article but are not steps of this argument.

nodes.label: We are directed to God as our end
That end surpasses reason's grasp
An end must be known to aim at it
Truths beyond reason must be made known
So revelation is necessary
Philosophy already covers all being
Do not seek things too high for you
Reason alone can reach every truth

hints: Aquinas's key move is about goals: what must be true of a goal before you can head toward it?
The route stays on the middle row. The boxes above and below come from the objections, not from Aquinas's answer.
After 'That end surpasses reason's grasp', the next step is about knowing an end before aiming at it.
activities.explanation: The route is: we are directed to God as our end → that end surpasses reason's grasp → an end must be known before we can direct our thoughts and actions to it → so truths beyond reason must be made known → so revelation is necessary. The upper detour ('Philosophy already covers all being' → 'Reason alone can reach every truth') is Objection 2's line of thought. It leads the other way, to the claim that no further knowledge is needed, so it cannot support Aquinas's conclusion. The lower detour ('Do not seek things too high for you') is the Bible verse quoted in Objection 1. In his reply Aquinas agrees that reason should not go hunting for such things, but he adds that once God reveals them they must be accepted by faith. That is a reply to the objection, not a step of this argument. Note that this route is only his first reason. The second reason (few people, long time, many errors) is a separate route to the same conclusion.

activities.title: Two kinds of truth about God
activities.prompt: Aquinas's two reasons cover two kinds of truth. Sort each one: is it beyond reason altogether, or within reason's reach but hard to get to?

groups.label: Beyond reason: only revelation can tell us
Within reason, but hard to reach

cards.text: What God has prepared for those who wait for Him (the verse from Isaiah that Aquinas quotes)
cards.feedback: Beyond reason. Aquinas quotes this verse because no eye has seen it: it is the clearest example of the end that 'surpasses the grasp of his reason'.

cards.text: What the philosophers knew of God by studying the things He made (Article 6)
cards.feedback: Within reason. Article 6 says God can be known 'through creatures just as philosophers knew Him'. Reason reached this, but by Aquinas's second reason only a few reached it, slowly and with errors.

cards.text: The truths about God in the part of philosophy Aristotle called theology
cards.feedback: Within reason. Objection 2 points to this 'divine science' to argue that philosophy is enough. Aquinas does not deny it exists. He says revelation is still needed, because few reach it unaided.

cards.text: That Christ rose from the dead, an article of faith (Article 8)
cards.feedback: Beyond reason. Article 8 says the articles of faith cannot be proved by human reason. They are received from revelation and then used as starting points for further argument.

cards.text: God as He is known to Himself alone (Article 6)
cards.feedback: Beyond reason. Article 6 sets this apart from what philosophers could know through creatures. It reaches us only if it is 'revealed to others'.

cards.text: A truth about God that reason can prove, though few would ever work it out
cards.feedback: Within reason. This is exactly the second kind. Reason could discover it, so it is not beyond reason. Aquinas still thinks revelation is needed so that it reaches everyone, sooner and without errors.

activities.takeaway: The first reason covers truths reason can never reach. The second covers truths reason can reach, but only for a few, after a long time and with mistakes. Revelation is needed for both, for different reasons.

activities.question: Which passage gives Aquinas's second reason: that even truths reason could reach would, without revelation, be known by few, late and with errors?

options.quote: Firstly, indeed, because man is directed to God, as to an end that surpasses the grasp of his reason
options.feedback: This is the first reason. It is about truths beyond reason, not about truths reason could reach but rarely does.

options.quote: because the truth about God such as reason could discover, would only be known by a few, and that after a long time, and with the admixture of many errors.
options.feedback: Correct. It names truths 'reason could discover' and lists the three problems: few people, a long time, and many errors.

options.quote: Although those things which are beyond man's knowledge may not be sought for by man through his reason, nevertheless, once they are revealed by God, they must be accepted by faith.
options.feedback: This is the reply to Objection 1. It concerns truths beyond reason and how to receive them, so it does not give the second reason.

options.quote: Hence there is no reason why those things which may be learned from philosophical science, so far as they can be known by natural reason, may not also be taught us by another science so far as they fall within revelation.
options.feedback: This is from the reply to Objection 2, the earlier idea that one truth can be known by two routes. It shows that revelation can teach what reason also knows, but not why that is needed. The 'few, long time, errors' passage gives the why.

hints: Look for a passage about truths reason could discover, not truths beyond reason.
The right passage lists three problems with leaving such truths to reason alone.

concepts.title: A science can borrow its starting points
concepts.idea: A science may start from principles proven by a higher science and take them on trust, as music does from arithmetic, and sacred doctrine takes its principles from God's knowledge in the same way.

terms.means: A starting point of a science: something it assumes and reasons from, rather than proves
Seen to be true as soon as it is understood, by the mind's own 'natural light', with no proof needed
A science whose proven results another science takes as its own starting points
The core beliefs of the Christian creed, which Aquinas treats as the principles of sacred doctrine

concepts.recap: A science's starting points need not be obvious: it can borrow them from a higher science, as music trusts arithmetic, and Aquinas says sacred doctrine borrows from God's knowledge.

understand.explanation: In this text a 'science' means any organised body of knowledge that reasons from starting points to conclusions; it does not mean lab work, and each starting point is called a principle. Some sciences, like arithmetic and geometry, start from self-evident principles, which the mind sees are true as soon as it understands them. Others start from results proven in a higher science and simply take them on trust: music (in the Middle Ages, the study of harmony as number ratios) borrows from arithmetic, and perspective (the study of sight lines) borrows from geometry. Aquinas says sacred doctrine is the second kind: its principles, the articles of faith, come from the knowledge God has and shares with the blessed in heaven, and they reach us by revelation. This is his answer to the worry that faith's starting points are not obvious to everyone. Keep in mind that this is Aquinas's argument, not a settled result, and the analogy has a limit: a musician could go and study arithmetic, but on Aquinas's view no one in this life can check God's knowledge directly, which is one reason later thinkers argued over whether theology is a science in the strict sense.
understand.quote: So it is that sacred doctrine is a science because it proceeds from principles established by the light of a higher science, namely, the science of God and the blessed. Hence, just as the musician accepts on authority the principles taught him by the mathematician, so sacred science is established on principles revealed by God.

activities.title: The musician trusts the mathematician

steps.text: Start at the top. Arithmetic begins from points the mind sees directly, by its 'natural light'. Nothing above it has to prove them for it.
From those starting points, arithmetic proves results about numbers and the ratios between them.
Medieval music studied harmonies as ratios of numbers. It does not prove arithmetic's results again. It takes them as its own starting points.

In Aquinas's words, the musician 'accepts on authority the principles taught him by the mathematician'. Music is still a real science, because it reasons carefully from those borrowed points to its own conclusions.
The same shape shows up elsewhere. Perspective, the study of sight lines, borrows its starting points from geometry.
Aquinas then applies the shape to faith. Sacred doctrine takes its principles, the articles of faith, from 'the science of God and the blessed', and these are made known to us by revelation.
steps.result: Sacred doctrine: borrows from God's knowledge

steps.text: So 'not self-evident to us' need not mean 'not a science'. It can mean 'borrowed from higher up'.

activities.takeaway: Aquinas names two ways for a science to get its starting points: see them directly, or take them from a higher science. Sacred doctrine, he argues, takes the second way, and its higher science is God's own knowledge.

activities.title: An everyday version: the builder and the engineer's table

steps.text: An engineer uses heavy maths to work out how much weight each kind of beam can carry, and prints the results as a table.
A builder planning a roof looks up the table and picks a beam. The builder has not checked the maths.
Still, the plan is reasoned, not guessed. The builder reasons correctly from the table to a safe roof.
But the roof is only as safe as the table. Borrowed starting points are only as reliable as their source.

activities.takeaway: Borrowing starting points from someone who knows more is normal and can still give real knowledge. Its strength depends on the source. That is why Aquinas stresses that sacred doctrine's source is God's knowledge, not a human expert.

activities.prompt: Match each science to where its starting points come from, as Aquinas describes it in Article 2.

pairs.feedback: Right. Aquinas says music proceeds 'from principles established by arithmetic'. The musician takes them on the mathematician's authority.
Right. Aquinas says perspective 'proceeds from principles established by geometry'. It is his second example of a borrowing science.

pairs.target: The science of God and the blessed
pairs.feedback: Right. Its principles are not proven by any human science. They come from the knowledge God has and shares with the blessed, and reach us by revelation.
Right. These are Aquinas's examples of sciences whose principles are 'known by the natural light of intelligence'. They borrow from no higher science.

activities.takeaway: Two sciences borrow from human sciences above them, two start from what the mind sees directly, and sacred doctrine borrows from a source above every human science.
hints: Ask of each one: does it prove its own starting points, or take them from somewhere above it?
Music deals with number ratios, and perspective deals with lines and angles.
Only one item on the left needs a source above every human science.

activities.prompt: Trace where sacred doctrine's starting points come from, step by step, from the bottom up to their highest source. Some routes are tempting but are not Aquinas's account.

Revelation to prophets and apostles
Knowledge of God and the blessed

activities.explanation: Sacred doctrine reasons from the articles of faith. These are not self-evident to everyone, and Objection 1 points this out: 'all men have not faith'. They are made known by revelation, and their highest source is the science of God and the blessed. Going through philosophy is the wrong route: Aquinas says sacred doctrine 'accepts its principles not from other sciences, but immediately from God, by revelation' (Article 5). It may use philosophy to explain things more clearly, but it does not get its starting points there. Going through later Church teachers is also wrong: in Article 8 he says faith rests on the revelation made to the apostles and prophets, not on revelations to other teachers.
hints: Sacred doctrine reasons from its principles. What are they called?
Objection 1 already says these principles are not admitted by all, and Article 5 rules out borrowing them from other sciences.
The route runs through what was revealed to the writers of Scripture.

activities.question: Objection 1 in Article 2 says: every science starts from self-evident principles. The articles of faith are not self-evident, since not everyone accepts them. So sacred doctrine is not a science. Which reply matches Aquinas's own answer?

options.text: A science's principles are either self-evident or taken from a higher science. Sacred doctrine's principles are taken from God's knowledge, just as music takes its principles from arithmetic.
options.feedback: Correct. This is his Reply to Objection 1: principles are 'either in themselves self-evident, or reducible to the conclusions of a higher science', and sacred doctrine's are the second kind. He rejects the objection's first claim that every science must start from self-evident principles.

options.text: The articles of faith really are self-evident to anyone who thinks carefully enough.
options.feedback: Not his answer. Aquinas grants that the articles are not admitted by all. He does not claim they are obvious. He claims they are borrowed from a higher science.

options.text: Sacred doctrine is not strictly a science, but that does not matter for faith.
options.feedback: Not his answer. Aquinas opens Article 2 with 'Sacred doctrine is a science.' He keeps the label and widens the idea of where a science's principles can come from.

options.text: Philosophy proves the articles of faith, so sacred doctrine borrows its principles from philosophy.
options.feedback: Not his answer. The borrowing pattern is right, but the source is wrong. In Article 5 he says sacred doctrine accepts its principles 'not from other sciences, but immediately from God, by revelation'. Philosophy only helps make its teaching clearer.

hints: Does Aquinas deny that the articles are not obvious to everyone, or does he accept it?
Look again at what he says the musician does with the mathematician's results.
His reply names two possible sources for a science's principles, not one.

concepts.title: One science, one way of looking
concepts.idea: A science is one when it treats everything under one aspect, just as sight takes in a man, a donkey and a stone because all are coloured, so sacred doctrine is one because it treats everything as revealed and as related to God.

terms.means: A settled, learned ability of the mind, such as knowing a science; Aquinas pairs it with 'faculty', a natural power like sight
The things themselves that a power or science deals with, such as men, donkeys and stones
The one aspect under which a power or science takes in all its things, such as 'being coloured' for sight

concepts.recap: A science is unified by the one aspect it looks through, not by how many kinds of thing it covers, so sacred doctrine stays one by treating everything as revealed and related to God.

understand.explanation: You might think a science is one because it studies one kind of thing, but Aquinas says a natural power or a habit (a settled, learned ability, such as knowing a science) is unified differently. What counts is not the heap of things it covers, its material object, but the single aspect under which it takes them in, its formal object. Your eyes see a man, a donkey and a stone, three very different things, yet sight is one power because it grasps all three only as coloured. In the same way, sacred doctrine covers God, angels, bodies and human conduct, but it treats each only as divinely revealed and as related to God, who is their beginning and end, so it stays one science. This is an argument by analogy, not a test, and it only works if you grant Aquinas's starting point that revelation is a real source of knowledge.
understand.quote: The unity of a faculty or habit is to be gauged by its object, not indeed, in its material aspect, but as regards the precise formality under which it is an object. For example, man, ass, stone agree in the one precise formality of being colored; and color is the formal object of sight.

activities.prompt: Put the three cases from Article 3 side by side. In each one, look at two things: the many items covered, and the single aspect that holds them together.

cases.label: Sight
cases.text: Covers: a man, a donkey (the translation says 'ass'), a stone. These are a person, an animal and a lifeless thing. One aspect: all three are coloured. Sight takes in nothing except as coloured, so it is one power.

cases.label: The 'common sense'
cases.text: Aquinas's name for the inner power that gathers what all five senses report. Covers: colours, sounds, smells, tastes, textures. One aspect: whatever affects the senses. It is one power, yet it reaches the objects of five different senses.

cases.label: Sacred doctrine
cases.text: Covers: God, angels, bodies, human morals, even the deeds of Abraham. One aspect: each is treated as divinely revealed and as related to God, its beginning or end. It treats God first, and creatures only so far as they point to him.

activities.takeaway: In every case the list of things is long and mixed, but the way of looking is single. Unity sits in the way of looking.

activities.prompt: An everyday picture, made up only to illustrate (it is not from the text): two books that both mention eggs, fire and knives.

cases.label: A cookbook
cases.text: It mentions eggs (biology), heat (physics) and knife skills (craft). Yet it is clearly one book, because it treats every item only as something used for cooking.

cases.label: A random scrapbook
cases.text: It holds a page on eggs, a page on fire safety and a page on knife collecting, each written for its own reason. Nothing ties the pages together, so it feels like three books glued into one cover.

activities.takeaway: The cookbook is like sacred doctrine in Aquinas's argument: mixed topics, one angle. The analogy is loose: Aquinas is speaking of a science, not a book.

activities.title: Same topic, which way of looking?
activities.prompt: Sort each card by the aspect under which the topic is being treated. The same subject can turn up in both groups; what decides is the angle.

groups.label: Treated as revealed and related to God (sacred doctrine)
Treated by natural reason alone (a philosophical science)

cards.text: Angels, as Scripture makes them known
cards.feedback: Article 3 names angels as a topic of sacred doctrine. Here they are taken up because they are revealed, which is its one aspect.

cards.text: The shape of the earth and the stars, worked out by an astronomer using mathematics
cards.feedback: Article 1 uses the astronomer as an example of a science that knows by natural reason. Nothing here is treated as revealed.

cards.text: Human acts, studied as the way a person is directed toward God as their end
cards.feedback: Article 4 says sacred doctrine treats human acts 'inasmuch as man is ordained by them to the perfect knowledge of God'. That reference to God is its aspect.

cards.text: Human acts, analysed by a moral philosopher from reason and experience alone
cards.feedback: Same topic as the previous card, but a different angle. Moral philosophy belongs to the 'separate philosophical sciences' mentioned in Article 3.

cards.text: God's existence, reasoned out by a philosopher from the world he made
cards.feedback: Even God can be studied this way: Article 1 calls it the theology that is 'part of philosophy' and says it 'differs in kind' from sacred doctrine, because the route is reason, not revelation.

cards.text: Bodies and the material world, as made by God and pointing back to him
cards.feedback: Article 3 lists 'corporeal creatures' as a topic. Creatures belong here only 'so far as they are referable to God as their beginning or end'.

cards.text: The deeds of Abraham, told as examples for living and as a link in the chain of revelation
cards.feedback: Article 2 says such individual facts enter as examples to follow and to establish the authority of those through whom revelation came, so they fall under the revealed aspect.

hints: Ignore the subject named on the card and ask how it is being looked at.
If the card mentions Scripture, revelation or a relation to God as beginning or end, it is the sacred aspect.
activities.takeaway: Angels, bodies, human acts and even God can each be studied in more than one way. A science's unity comes from the angle it takes, not from owning a list of subjects.

activities.question: An objector in Article 3 says: sacred doctrine deals with angels, bodies and human morals, which belong to separate philosophical sciences, so it cannot be one science. How does Aquinas answer?

options.text: It treats all of them under one aspect, so far as they can be included in revelation, so its unity is not broken.
options.feedback: Correct. Like the 'common sense', which is one power reaching the objects of all five senses, sacred doctrine reaches many topics through one aspect: their being revealed and related to God.

options.text: It treats God and creatures equally, so it is simply a larger science that contains all the smaller ones.
options.feedback: Not quite. Aquinas says it does 'not treat of God and creatures equally, but of God primarily'. Unity comes from the shared aspect, not from adding sciences together.

options.text: It does not really deal with angels, bodies or morals; the objector has misread it.
options.feedback: No. Aquinas accepts that it treats these topics. He denies only that covering them splits the science, because it treats them from one angle.

options.text: Angels, bodies and morals are really one kind of thing, so the science studies only one kind of thing.
options.feedback: This has the test backwards. A man, a donkey and a stone are not one kind of thing either. Unity comes from the formal object, the shared aspect, not from the things being alike.

hints: Recall the man, the donkey and the stone: are they one kind of thing?
Look for the option that puts unity in the way of looking, not in the things looked at.

activities.question: Article 7 reports that some teachers said this science's subject was 'things and signs', or 'the works of salvation', or 'the whole Christ'. Where does Aquinas say they went wrong?

options.text: They looked at what is treated in the science, not at the aspect under which it is treated.
options.feedback: Correct. Aquinas says the science does treat all those things, 'but so far as they have reference to God'. They named the material object, the things covered, and missed the formal object.

options.text: Those topics never appear in sacred doctrine at all.
options.feedback: No. Aquinas says plainly: 'Of all these things, in truth, we treat in this science.' His quarrel is about the angle, not the list.

options.text: They were right, and Aquinas agrees that the subject is not God.
options.feedback: No. Aquinas concludes that 'God is in very truth the object of this science', because all things are treated under the aspect of God. This is a real disagreement in the text, and he takes a side.

hints: Recall the two kinds of object: the things covered, and the aspect they are seen under.

concepts.title: Not all authorities weigh the same
concepts.idea: An argument from human authority is the weakest kind, but one from divine revelation is the strongest, so Scripture counts as decisive, Church teachers as probable, and philosophers as outside but probable support.

terms.means: Accepting a claim because of who vouches for it, not because you checked it yourself
The books the Church accepts as belonging to the inspired Bible
Settling a question so that it cannot be overturned
Likely and worth real weight, but not final; it could in principle be wrong

concepts.recap: Who vouches decides the weight: God's revelation in canonical Scripture is decisive, while Church teachers and philosophers, being human, give only probable support.

understand.explanation: An argument from authority means accepting a claim because of who vouches for it, the way you trust a doctor's word about a medicine without testing it yourself. Aquinas grants that when the one vouching is only human, this is the weakest kind of argument, because humans can be wrong; but when God vouches through revelation (God making truths known), it is the strongest, because God cannot be wrong. So he ranks his sources: the canonical Scriptures, the books the Church accepts as the inspired Bible, are incontrovertible, meaning they settle a question for good. The doctors of the Church (its great teachers, such as Augustine) may properly be used but are only probable: likely and weighty, yet not final. Philosophers such as Aristotle also count where natural reason let them see the truth, but only as extrinsic (coming from outside sacred doctrine) and probable support. The reason given is that faith rests on the revelation made to the writers of Scripture, not on any later teacher, however holy; this ranking is argued from inside Christian belief, so following its logic does not require sharing that belief.
understand.quote: Nevertheless, sacred doctrine makes use of these authorities as extrinsic and probable arguments; but properly uses the authority of the canonical Scriptures as an incontrovertible proof, and the authority of the doctors of the Church as one that may properly be used, yet merely as probable.

activities.prompt: Put these three kinds of authority in order, from the most weight Aquinas gives them to the least.
items: The canonical Scriptures: used as an incontrovertible proof
The doctors of the Church: may properly be used, yet merely as probable
The philosophers: used as extrinsic and probable arguments
activities.explanation: Scripture comes first because it carries God's revelation, which cannot mislead, so it is decisive. Church teachers and philosophers are both only probable, because both are human. Aquinas still sets them apart: the Church's teachers may 'properly' be used, since they work inside sacred doctrine, while philosophers are 'extrinsic', helpers from outside who count only on questions natural reason can reach. The gap between the first rung and the other two is a gap in kind (divine against human), not just in size.
hints: Ask who ultimately vouches for each source: God, or a human being.
Two of the three are called 'probable'. What word does Aquinas add to tell them apart?
'Properly used' marks a source inside sacred doctrine; 'extrinsic' marks one from outside it.

activities.title: Decisive or probable?
activities.prompt: Each card is a source Aquinas actually quotes somewhere in Question 1. Using his own rule, sort each by the weight it would carry as an argument.

cards.text: 2 Timothy 3:16: "All Scripture, inspired of God is profitable to teach, to reprove, to correct, to instruct in justice."
cards.feedback: A letter in the New Testament, so it is canonical Scripture and counts as decisive.

cards.text: Isaiah 64:4: "The eye hath not seen, O God, besides Thee, what things Thou hast prepared for them that wait for Thee."
cards.feedback: A book of the prophets, one of the writers to whom Aquinas says revelation was made, so it is canonical and decisive.

cards.text: Titus 1:9: a bishop should be able "to convince the gainsayers."
cards.feedback: Another New Testament letter, so it is canonical Scripture. Being short or practical in tone does not lower its weight; what counts is where it comes from.

cards.text: Augustine (De Trin. xiv, 1): "to this science alone belongs that whereby saving faith is begotten, nourished, protected and strengthened."
cards.feedback: Augustine is a doctor of the Church. He may properly be used, but merely as probable. Aquinas quotes Augustine himself saying that only the canonical books are free of error, while other authors must be read critically.

cards.text: Ambrose (De Fide 1): "Put arguments aside where faith is sought."
cards.feedback: Ambrose is a Church teacher, so he counts as probable. This quote appears in an objection, and Aquinas goes on to answer it: a holy teacher's words can still be weighed and qualified.

cards.text: Dionysius (Coel. Hier. i): "We cannot be enlightened by the divine rays except they be hidden within the covering of many sacred veils."
cards.feedback: Aquinas leans on Dionysius often and with great respect, but Dionysius is a Christian writer, not a canonical author. Frequent use does not lift a source to the level of Scripture.

cards.text: Aristotle (Metaph. vi): there is a part of philosophy called theology, or the divine science.
cards.feedback: Aristotle is a philosopher, so his authority is extrinsic and probable. It counts only on matters natural reason can reach, and Aquinas uses it here inside an objection that he later answers.

cards.text: Aratus, as quoted by Paul: "For we are also His offspring."
cards.feedback: This is the tricky one. The line appears in Acts 17:28, but Aquinas offers it as his example of using 'the authority of philosophers' who knew a truth by natural reason. The words are a pagan poet's, so as Aratus's authority they count only as probable, even though Paul repeats them.

activities.takeaway: The test is not how wise, holy or often cited a source is, but whether it carries God's revelation. Only canonical Scripture settles a question; every human voice, saint or pagan, supports it only probably.
hints: For each card, ask: is this a book of the Bible, or a human writer?
Holiness and fame do not move a card into the decisive group in Aquinas's scheme.
One card is a poet's line that a Bible writer quotes. Whose authority is Aquinas pointing to when he cites it?

activities.question: Which passage explains why even a holy Church teacher counts only as probable, while Scripture counts as decisive?

options.quote: For our faith rests upon the revelation made to the apostles and prophets who wrote the canonical books, and not on the revelations (if any such there are) made to other doctors.
options.feedback: Correct. This places the revelation that faith rests on in the canonical writers alone. A later teacher, however holy, is not where that revelation lives, so his word stays human and probable.

options.quote: for although the argument from authority based on human reason is the weakest, yet the argument from authority based on divine revelation is the strongest.
options.feedback: Close, and it is the root principle of the ranking: human authority is weakest, divine authority strongest. But on its own it does not say where divine revelation is found, so it cannot yet explain why Augustine falls below Scripture. The chosen passage supplies that missing step.

options.quote: Hence the fact that some happen to doubt about articles of faith is not due to the uncertain nature of the truths, but to the weakness of human intelligence
options.feedback: This passage, from Article 5, explains why people doubt the articles of faith, not how to weigh different sources against each other. It says nothing about Church teachers or Scripture.

options.quote: Since therefore grace does not destroy nature but perfects it, natural reason should minister to faith as the natural bent of the will ministers to charity.
options.feedback: This explains why sacred doctrine may use human reason at all, which is why philosophers get a place. It does not explain the gap between Scripture and the Church's teachers.

hints: Look for a passage that names where the revelation behind faith was given.
The right passage mentions both the writers of the canonical books and 'other doctors'.

concepts.title: Argue from your principles, not to them
concepts.idea: Sacred doctrine reasons from its principles to new conclusions; it can argue with someone who grants some revealed truths, but with someone who grants none it can only answer objections, which are never real proofs against faith.

terms.means: The basic truths of the Christian creed, received from revelation. They are the starting points (principles) of sacred doctrine.
A strict proof from true premises whose conclusion must follow, so it cannot be wrong.
The highest branch of philosophy, which studies being itself. No philosophical science sits above it.
Someone who accepts Scripture but rejects some teaching drawn from it.

concepts.recap: Theology, like music, starts from principles it does not prove. It argues from them, not to them, and with someone who grants none of them it can only answer objections.

understand.explanation: Every science starts from principles it does not prove inside itself. Sacred doctrine takes its principles, the articles of faith, on trust from God's knowledge, as music takes its rules from arithmetic. So Aquinas says it argues from its principles, not to them, as Paul argues from Christ's resurrection to the resurrection of all the dead. When someone denies a principle, sacred doctrine is placed like metaphysics, the highest branch of philosophy: no higher science defends its principles, so it can debate only an opponent who concedes something. With a heretic, who accepts Scripture but rejects some teaching, it argues from Scripture texts; with someone who grants no revealed truth, it cannot prove the articles by reasoning and can only answer objections. Aquinas adds that such an objection is never a demonstration, a strict proof whose conclusion must follow, because faith rests on infallible truth, a reason that only works for someone who already accepts that premise.
understand.quote: As other sciences do not argue in proof of their principles, but argue from their principles to demonstrate other truths in these sciences: so this doctrine does not argue in proof of its principles, which are the articles of faith, but from them it goes on to prove something else

activities.title: Paul's resurrection argument, step by step

steps.text: Start with a principle that Paul's readers already accept from revelation: Christ rose from the dead.
steps.result: Principle: taken on faith, not proved here

steps.text: Paul does not try to prove Christ's resurrection from something more basic. In this argument it is the fixed starting point, one of the articles of faith.

From it he draws a new conclusion: the dead in general will rise. Aquinas only names this argument (1 Corinthians 15). One way to spell out the link: if no dead person could rise, Christ could not have risen; Christ did rise; so the dead can rise.
Compare an everyday science. A geometry class proves theorems from axioms, but it never proves the axioms in that class. Music, as we saw, takes its rules from arithmetic on trust.
So the argument runs in one direction: from the principles down to new conclusions. It never runs back up to prove the principles themselves.

activities.takeaway: Sacred doctrine argues from the articles of faith to further truths. It does not argue to the articles of faith.

activities.title: When someone denies a principle

steps.text: A lower science does not defend its own principles. It leaves that job to the higher science it borrows them from, as music would leave a dispute about numbers to arithmetic.
Metaphysics, the highest branch of philosophy, has no science above it to pass the job to. It can debate someone who denies its principles, but only if that person concedes something to start from.
If the opponent concedes nothing at all, metaphysics cannot argue with them. It can still answer their objections.

Sacred doctrine also has no science above it, so it is in the same position. With a heretic, who accepts Scripture but rejects some teaching, it argues from texts of Scripture. Against someone who denies one article of faith, it argues from another article they still accept.
With someone who believes nothing of revelation, there is no shared starting point. It cannot prove the articles by reasoning. It can only answer the objections they raise.

Aquinas's last step: faith rests on infallible truth, and the opposite of a truth can never be demonstrated. So an argument against faith is never a demonstration, a strict proof. It is only a difficulty that can be answered.

activities.takeaway: This is the lesson's main point. Theology can be a real science without proving its own starting points, just as music borrows from arithmetic. It argues from those starting points, not to them, and against someone who grants none of them it can only answer objections.

activities.prompt: An opponent believes nothing of divine revelation and raises an objection to an article of faith. Trace, in order, the route Aquinas says sacred doctrine must take.

nodes.label: Opponent denies an article of faith
Do they grant any revealed truth?
Yes: argue from what they grant
Heretic: argue from Scripture texts
No: they grant nothing revealed
Prove the article by pure reason
Cannot prove the articles by reason
Can only answer their objections
Objections: answerable difficulties

activities.explanation: This opponent grants no revealed truth, so the upper branch is closed. That branch means arguing from shared texts, as with a heretic. The branch 'Prove the article by pure reason' is a trap: Aquinas says there is 'no longer any means of proving the articles of faith by reasoning'. What is left is answering objections, and he holds that those objections are never demonstrations, only difficulties that can be answered.
hints: First ask: what does this opponent grant?
They grant nothing revealed, so you go down, not up.
Avoid the branch that claims reason alone can prove an article of faith.

activities.title: What can be done with each person?
activities.prompt: These people are made up to illustrate Aquinas's rule. Sort each one by what sacred doctrine can do with them.

groups.label: No dispute: reason from principles to new truths
Argue from revealed truths they grant

cards.text: A believer asks what follows from Christ's resurrection for everyone else.
cards.feedback: No principle is under attack. This is the normal work of the science, going from an article of faith to a new conclusion, as Paul did.

cards.text: Someone accepts the Gospels as revealed but denies one article of faith.
cards.feedback: They still grant other articles. Aquinas says that 'against those who deny one article of faith, we can argue from another.'

cards.text: A heretic who reads Scripture as God's word but rejects one teaching drawn from it.
cards.feedback: Scripture is common ground, so this is Aquinas's own example: 'we can argue with heretics from texts in Holy Writ.'

cards.text: A sceptic who accepts no revelation at all and says miracles are impossible.
cards.feedback: There is no shared revealed premise to argue from. Aquinas says one can then only answer the objections, not prove the articles.

cards.text: A philosopher who trusts natural reason only and grants no revealed truth.
cards.feedback: Being clever or reasonable does not create common ground. What matters is whether they grant any revealed truth, and this one grants none.

cards.text: Someone who accepts the Old Testament as revealed but not the New.
cards.feedback: They admit 'some at least of the truths obtained through divine revelation', which is Aquinas's condition for real argument. This case is our application of his rule, not an example he gives here.

activities.takeaway: The deciding question is not how intelligent or hostile the person is. It is whether they grant any revealed truth: some means argue, none means only answer objections.
hints: For each person, ask: is anyone denying a principle at all?
If someone is, ask whether they grant any revealed truth, even just a part of it.

activities.question: Aquinas says arguments against faith 'cannot be demonstrations, but are difficulties that can be answered.' What does this claim actually establish?

options.text: That reason can prove the articles of faith true to anyone.
options.feedback: No. In the same passage he says that against someone who believes nothing of revelation there is 'no longer any means of proving the articles of faith by reasoning'.

options.text: That if faith rests on infallible truth, no sound strict proof can conclude against it, so every objection must contain a flaw somewhere.
options.feedback: Yes. The claim is conditional. It follows from his premise that 'faith rests upon infallible truth' together with the rule that the contrary of a truth cannot be demonstrated. It is a defence, not a proof of the articles.

options.text: That every sceptic will be persuaded once their objections are answered.
options.feedback: No. Answering an objection removes one difficulty. It does not supply the missing premise. Aquinas never promises the sceptic will come to believe.

options.text: That everyone, believer or not, must accept that objections to faith are weak.
options.feedback: No. The claim rests on a premise, that faith is infallible truth, which someone who rejects revelation does not grant. So its force reaches only those who accept that premise.

hints: Look at the reason Aquinas gives: what premise does it rest on?
Ask whether a person who rejects revelation shares that premise.

activities.question: An imagined reader who does not accept revelation says: 'Claiming every objection can be answered assumes the very thing we disagree about.' How should we read Aquinas's claim in light of this?

options.text: As a claim made from inside the faith. It tells the believing theologian how to treat objections, not why a sceptic should accept the articles.
options.feedback: Well supported. His reason, that faith rests on infallible truth, is a premise only believers grant. His own scheme says that with such an opponent he can only answer objections, so he does not claim to convince them. Limit: Aquinas does not see it as a mere rule of thumb. He holds it to be true.

options.text: As circular, and therefore worthless.
options.feedback: Partly supported. The reader is right that the claim depends on the premise in dispute. But Aquinas does not offer it as a proof to the sceptic, so the charge of circular proof misses what he claims. It still does real work: it tells the theologian to examine each objection for a flaw rather than simply accept it.

options.text: As a promise that every objection has already been answered.
options.feedback: Not supported by the text. Aquinas says the objections 'are difficulties that can be answered', meaning in principle. He does not say answers already exist for all of them, or that they will satisfy everyone. This misreads his words.

hints: Separate two questions: is the claim true for Aquinas, and should a sceptic be moved by it?
Recall what Aquinas says is possible with someone who grants no revealed truth.
